audit.action: cite a better source for the same coding
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: Rasch 2002:9 quotation confirmed verbatim in the held scanned/PDF (PDF p. 29 = book p. 9); template on pp. 4-6 as described. (2) Deciding source is a 2002 Rice dissertation (grammar-type, 393 pp) whose phonology chapter gives the structural fact (only the final vowel of a phonological word is full and tone-bearing) rather than an explicit stress rule; the StressTyp2 layer rests on a 1965 comparative article we do not hold. But two HELD primaries state the rule outright and were not used: Pride 1965 Chatino Syntax (Yaitepec) p. 248 'word stress always occurring on the ultimate syllable', and Pride & Pride 2004 Diccionario chatino de la zona alta pp. xiii and 346 'Todas las palabras chatinas se pronuncian con mayor fuerza en la última sílaba'. All held and fetched sources agree: fixed final prominence, no weight sensitivity, no exceptions in native vocabulary; Spanish loans are restr

sources.quote: Rasch 2002:9: "I understand the distribution of the reduced vowels to be a result of a historical process in which unstressed vowels first gradually harmonized with the following environment. ... in a single phonological word, only one vowel (the final one) is unreduced." Also Rasch 2002:4-5 (Table 3 / Figure 1): the phonological word template (n/nw.)(C(V[reduced]).)CV(7)(n) — every non-final vowel is reduced/unstressed, the final vowel alone is full and tone-bearing. sources.note: Glottolog's top-ranked phonology for west2644 (379 pp) and the only full phonology of a ctp variety; record rested on a morphosyntax dissertation's 9-page phonology chapter. fetched sources: confirms loss of all non-tonic (non-final) syllables in simplex words; no competing stress rule.

sources.citation: Cruz, Emiliana & Anthony C. Woodbury. 2014. Finding a way into a family of tone languages: The story and methods of the Chatino Language Documentation Project. Language Documentation & Conservation 8: 490-524.
sources.quote: p. 495: 'As in YAI [Yaitepec], words (except compounds and certain loans) were monosyllabic; and each monosyllabic word bore one of apparently very many distinct tones'; p. 511: 'SJQ and PAN [Panixtlahuaca] have reduced all words to monosyllables by losing all vowels and some consonants from non-final syllables, and by losing distinctive vowel length; while ZAC and ZEN retain the conservative Chatino prosodic patterns'.
sources.note: States the prosodic word shape of exactly the three ctp varieties (YAI, SJQ, PAN): simplex words monosyllabic, non-final syllables lost — needed for the domain/caution note on a 'fixed final' coding.

sources.quote: Survey only: 'Stress is usually fixed in Oto-Manguean languages, and is always confined to roots/stems ... root-initial and root-final stress are the norm'; Zapotecan row of Table 27.5 counts 8 languages with monosyllabic roots and 8 root-final; no per-language statement for any ctp variety in the chapter text. 'Little work has examined the phonetic correlates of stress in Oto-Manguean languages'.
